label: Java Full-Stack Fresher (0–1 Year)
description: Complete Java Full-Stack interview preparation for freshers and entry-level developers. Covers Core Java, DSA, Spring Boot, SQL, HTML/CSS, JavaScript, React, Fullstack Integration, Design basics, DevOps tools, and Behavioral.

modules.title: Core Java & OOP Fundamentals
modules.intro: Core Java interview questions are the single most important section for every fresher interview. This module covers what every Java developer is expected to know on Day 1 — the four pillars of OOP (encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism, abstraction), exception handling (checked vs unchecked, try-with-resources, custom exceptions), String immutability and the String pool, access modifiers, and the comparisons interviewers repeat in every session (== vs equals, abstract class vs interface, overloading vs overriding). Every answer is shaped around how you'd explain it in a 5-minute slot: headline, one-line why, a tiny code anchor, and the follow-up the interviewer is already composing.

modules.title: Java Collections Framework
modules.intro: Java Collections is one of the top-three most-asked sections in every fresher screening. Interviewers want to know whether you can pick the right data structure — ArrayList vs LinkedList, HashMap vs HashSet, PriorityQueue for heap problems — and whether you understand what's happening under the hood when you call put() or get(). This module covers the framework's core contracts (List, Set, Map, Queue), the implementation trade-offs that freshers are expected to articulate, the equals/hashCode contract that powers every Map and Set, and the iteration patterns that appear in every coding round.

modules.title: Java 8 Features — Lambdas, Streams & Optionals
modules.intro: Java 8 changed how Java developers write code, and interviewers now test these features even at the fresher level. Expect questions on what a lambda expression is and when to use it, the built-in functional interfaces (Function, Predicate, Consumer, Supplier), Stream terminal vs intermediate operations, Optional as a null-safe container, and method references. This module builds each concept from first principles — why were these added, what problem do they solve, and how would you use them in a real Spring Boot service method.

modules.title: Arrays & String Algorithms
modules.intro: Arrays and strings are the entry point for almost every fresher coding round — two-sum, valid anagram, longest substring without repeating characters, and their variations. This module covers the patterns interviewers recycle: two pointers (sorted arrays, palindrome checks), sliding window (subarray/substring optimisation), frequency maps (anagram detection, most frequent element), and prefix sums (range queries). Each pattern is taught with the 'why this pattern fits this shape of problem' reasoning, so you can adapt it under time pressure rather than memorising individual solutions.

modules.title: Linked Lists, Stacks & Queues
modules.intro: Linked list, stack, and queue problems come up in almost every fresher coding round because they test pointer manipulation and recursive thinking without needing complex math. This module covers the canonical operations (reverse a list, detect a cycle using fast/slow pointers, merge two sorted lists) and the stack/queue patterns (balanced parentheses, next greater element, sliding window maximum). For each problem the focus is on the mental model — draw the pointer diagram, identify the invariant, code the two-pointer dance — not just the answer.

modules.title: Trees & Binary Search Trees
modules.intro: Trees appear in roughly half of all fresher-to-junior coding rounds. The good news: most tree problems reduce to one of four traversal patterns — inorder, preorder, postorder, or BFS. This module walks through each traversal, then applies them to the problems interviewers love: validate a BST, find the lowest common ancestor, check if a tree is balanced, count nodes at each level. Every solution is shown recursively first (to build intuition), then iteratively with a stack/queue (to show you know both approaches).

modules.title: Graphs — BFS, DFS & Common Problems
modules.intro: Graph questions at the fresher level are almost always disguised matrix problems — number of islands, flood fill, course schedule (cycle detection), and word ladder. The underlying technique is always BFS or DFS with a visited set. This module teaches the template for each traversal, when to pick BFS (shortest path, level-by-level) vs DFS (cycle detection, path exploration), and the adjacency-list vs adjacency-matrix representation trade-off. Mastering graphs at this level means being able to recognise a graph problem that is dressed up as a 2D grid.

modules.title: Sorting, Searching, Recursion & Intro to DP
modules.intro: This module ties together the algorithmic thinking every fresher needs: sorting (know the trade-offs of merge sort vs quicksort vs insertion sort in interviews), binary search (the pattern, not just the textbook version — think search in rotated sorted array), recursion as a thinking tool, and the intro to dynamic programming through the classic coin-change / climbing-stairs / knapsack group. Big-O analysis is woven into every topic because every coding-round interviewer will ask 'what's the time complexity' — this module makes that question trivial to answer.

modules.title: Spring Core & Spring Boot Basics
modules.intro: Spring Boot is the default backend framework for Java fullstack development, and freshers are expected to know it well enough to bootstrap a REST API on their first week. This module covers the dependency injection mental model (why it exists, what it solves), the Spring component stereotypes (@Component, @Service, @Repository, @Controller) and when to use each, Spring Boot's auto-configuration magic and how to override it, profiles for environment management, and Actuator for basic health monitoring. Every concept is anchored to a practical 'here's what you'd write in a real project' example.

modules.title: Spring MVC & REST API Design
modules.intro: Building REST APIs with Spring MVC is the day-one job of a Java fullstack developer, and interviewers test whether you actually understand what REST means beyond 'it uses HTTP'. This module covers the six REST constraints and why they matter, the @RestController vs @Controller distinction, how @GetMapping / @PostMapping / @PutMapping / @DeleteMapping map to HTTP semantics, Bean Validation with @Valid, and the global exception handling pattern with @ControllerAdvice that keeps error responses consistent. You'll also learn the HTTP status codes interviewers expect you to use correctly (201 vs 200, 400 vs 422, 401 vs 403).

modules.title: Spring Data JPA & Hibernate Basics
modules.intro: JPA and Hibernate are how Spring Boot applications talk to relational databases, and freshers are expected to know enough to design entity classes, define relationships, and write basic queries without generating N+1 problems. This module covers the @Entity / @Table / @Column annotations, the relationship mappings (@OneToMany, @ManyToOne, @ManyToMany) with their owning-side rules, Spring Data JPA's derived query mechanism (findByEmailAndActive), the difference between JPQL and native SQL in queries, and why lazy loading causes the single most common Spring Boot production bug — the LazyInitializationException.

modules.title: Spring Security & Authentication Basics
modules.intro: Security is not optional, and interviewers test whether freshers understand the difference between authentication (who are you?) and authorisation (what can you do?). This module covers the Spring Security filter chain at a conceptual level, JWT structure (header.payload.signature) and the end-to-end login flow, why passwords are hashed with BCrypt and not encrypted, stateless vs stateful session management, and role-based access control with @PreAuthorize. You don't need to know the full SecurityFilterChain API by heart — you need to be able to explain the flow coherently and know where to look when it breaks.

modules.title: SQL Fundamentals — Queries, Joins & Aggregations
modules.intro: SQL is tested in virtually every software engineering interview regardless of role, and freshers are expected to write correct multi-table queries under time pressure. This module covers SELECT with filtering and ordering, the JOIN family (INNER, LEFT, RIGHT, FULL OUTER — and the mental model for each), GROUP BY with HAVING, subqueries, and the string and date functions that come up in take-home tests. Every topic includes a 'write the query for this scenario' exercise because SQL interviews are almost always hands-on.

modules.title: Database Design, Indexes & ACID
modules.intro: Writing queries is only half of what interviewers test — they also want to know whether you can design a schema that won't fall apart under real usage. This module covers normalisation (why 3NF matters and when denormalisation is intentional), the primary/foreign key model, why indexes speed up reads and slow down writes, ACID properties and what they mean in a Spring Boot @Transactional context, and the trade-offs between different relationship cardinalities. The capstone exercise is a classic: design the schema for a library management system or an e-commerce order table.

modules.title: HTML5 & CSS3 Fundamentals
modules.intro: HTML and CSS are the skeleton and skin of every frontend application. Interviewers for fullstack roles test whether you know the semantic HTML elements that matter for SEO and accessibility (article vs section vs div), the box model, how the cascade and specificity work, and whether you can build a layout with Flexbox and CSS Grid without looking at documentation. This module covers the questions freshers get most often: inline vs block, position fixed vs sticky, how media queries work, and the common accessibility attributes (aria-label, role, tabindex) that mark a thoughtful frontend developer.

modules.title: JavaScript Core — ES6+ & Async Patterns
modules.intro: JavaScript is the language of the web, and fullstack Java developers are expected to be as comfortable in JS as in Java. This module covers the concepts freshers consistently underestimate: closures (why the counter increment works, and why the loop closure gotcha trips people up), how 'this' behaves in arrow functions vs regular functions, the event loop and why setTimeout(fn, 0) doesn't run immediately, and the async/await model built on top of Promises. Every concept is paired with the exact question an interviewer will ask: 'What is a closure?', 'What is the difference between == and ===?', 'Explain the event loop.'

modules.title: TypeScript Essentials for Java Developers
modules.intro: TypeScript is the default for any professional React or Angular codebase in 2024, and freshers who understand it have a clear edge. For Java developers, TypeScript feels familiar — it adds compile-time type safety to JavaScript the same way Java's type system works, but with structural rather than nominal typing. This module covers the concepts freshers are quizzed on: interface vs type alias, union vs intersection types, generics (and why they're weaker than Java generics due to type erasure at runtime), optional chaining, and how TypeScript integrates with React component props.

modules.title: React Core — Components, Props, State & Hooks
modules.intro: React is the most-used frontend library in fullstack Java projects, and freshers are expected to know it well enough to build a working CRUD UI. This module covers the React mental model (component tree, unidirectional data flow, virtual DOM diffing), functional components with hooks (useState for local state, useEffect for side effects and cleanup), the key prop and why React needs it for list reconciliation, and the event handling patterns that differ from vanilla JavaScript. Every answer is shaped around what a fresh React developer would say in a technical screen — not a veteran's deep internals dive.

modules.title: React Ecosystem — Router, Context, Forms & API Calls
modules.intro: Once you know React fundamentals, interviewers push into the ecosystem: how do you share state across components without passing props 12 levels deep (Context API), how do you navigate between pages (React Router), how do you call your Spring Boot API from React (fetch/axios inside useEffect, or a custom hook), and how do you keep forms manageable (controlled components with useState). This module covers these practical patterns alongside the performance hooks (useMemo, useCallback) that freshers often misunderstand, and custom hooks as the React idiom for reusable logic.

modules.title: REST API Integration — Frontend ↔ Backend
modules.intro: A fullstack developer must be able to connect a React frontend to a Spring Boot backend without being blocked by CORS errors, serialisation mismatches, or unhandled error states. This module covers the HTTP contract (what fetch() is actually sending, what the server is sending back), CORS preflight and how to configure Spring Boot's @CrossOrigin or WebMvcConfigurer, the JSON ↔ Java object mapping rules (Jackson), and the frontend patterns for showing loading spinners, retry buttons, and user-friendly error messages. The integrative perspective — trace a user action from button click to database write and back — is what distinguishes a fullstack developer from two separate specialists.

modules.title: Authentication — End-to-End Flow
modules.intro: Authentication is the fullstack integration topic freshers get quizzed on most. Interviewers want to know whether you understand the complete flow — user submits login form → Spring Boot validates credentials → issues JWT → React stores the token → React sends the token on every subsequent request → Spring Security validates it. This module traces that journey end to end, covers the JWT storage trade-off (localStorage is vulnerable to XSS; HttpOnly cookies are safer but need CSRF protection), how to protect React routes for logged-in users, and the refresh token pattern that keeps sessions alive without storing long-lived secrets.

modules.title: Design Patterns — GoF Essentials & SOLID
modules.intro: Design patterns are the vocabulary senior engineers use to describe solutions, and freshers who know them stand out immediately. This module focuses on the patterns that appear in Java and Spring Boot codebases every day — Singleton (and why Spring beans are singletons), Factory (how Spring creates beans), Builder (Lombok @Builder, StringBuilder), Strategy (payment method selection, sorting algorithms), and Observer (Spring events, React state callbacks). SOLID principles are taught as the diagnosis tool: when an interviewer asks you to improve a piece of code, naming which SOLID principle it violates is the clearest way to structure your answer.

modules.title: System Design Fundamentals — For Freshers
modules.intro: Freshers are not expected to design Twitter from scratch, but they are expected to understand the building blocks of web systems. This module covers the client-server model (what actually happens when you type a URL), HTTP fundamentals (request/response lifecycle, status codes, headers), the difference between SQL and NoSQL databases and when to use each, what caching is and why it matters (cache-aside pattern, Redis as a session store), and the intuition behind horizontal vs vertical scaling. These concepts are the foundation for the system design questions that scale with experience — getting them right at the fresher level shows architectural awareness.

modules.title: Git & Version Control Workflow
modules.intro: Git is the universal prerequisite for any development job, and interviewers both ask questions about it and observe how you work with it during the take-home or pair-programming round. This module covers the essential commands (add, commit, push, pull, fetch, merge, rebase, stash, reset), the branching strategies teams actually use (feature branches, Gitflow, trunk-based development), how pull requests and code review fit into the workflow, and how to resolve merge conflicts without panicking. The emphasis is on the workflow, not just the commands — knowing what merge vs rebase means for the team's history is the question that reveals real-world experience.

modules.title: Maven, Build Tools & Docker Basics
modules.intro: Freshers who can build and containerise their own Spring Boot application are immediately more employable than those who can't run it outside their IDE. This module covers Maven's build lifecycle (compile → test → package → verify → install → deploy), the pom.xml dependency management model, and the Maven vs Gradle trade-off. Docker is increasingly expected even at the fresher level: this module covers the container mental model (image vs container), writing a basic Dockerfile for a Spring Boot app, and using Docker Compose to run the backend + database together locally — exactly the setup you'd submit with a take-home project.

modules.title: Testing Fundamentals — JUnit, Mockito & Frontend Testing
modules.intro: Every professional development team writes tests, and freshers who can write a basic JUnit test for a service class and mock its dependencies with Mockito are noticeably ahead. This module covers the test pyramid (unit → integration → end-to-end) and why mocking makes sense at the unit level, JUnit 5 annotations (@Test, @BeforeEach, @AfterEach, @ParameterizedTest), Mockito's when/thenReturn and verify patterns, Spring Boot's @WebMvcTest and @DataJpaTest slices for integration testing, and a brief introduction to Jest and React Testing Library for the frontend side. You don't need to be a testing expert — you need to show you value it.

modules.title: Behavioral Interview & Engineering Practices
modules.intro: The behavioral round is where freshers win or lose offers they technically deserved. This module covers the STAR method (Situation, Task, Action, Result) as the backbone for every story question, how to walk an interviewer through a college project without making it sound trivial, the classic questions every fresher faces (tell me about yourself, what's your biggest weakness, describe a time you worked in a team), and the coding-round mindset — how to think out loud, how to ask clarifying questions before coding, and how to recover when you're stuck. The goal is to be the candidate who is equally credible in the technical and the human parts of the interview.

modules.title: Java Threading Basics
modules.intro: Java threading basics appear in almost every fresher interview — even when the role is fullstack. Interviewers want to know that you understand the difference between a process and a thread, can create a thread two ways (extending Thread vs implementing Runnable), know the six thread lifecycle states, and have a basic grasp of synchronized and visibility problems. This module stops before advanced concurrency (locks, CompletableFuture chains) — just the foundation every fresher needs to answer threading questions without going blank.

modules.title: Angular Basics for Fullstack Developers
modules.intro: Angular basics are expected in Java fullstack fresher interviews because most enterprise Java shops use Angular on the frontend. This module covers what freshers actually get asked: how Angular differs from React structurally (opinionated framework vs library, TypeScript-first, two-way binding by default), the Angular component/module mental model, the four types of data binding, the most common structural directives (*ngIf, *ngFor), how Angular's DI container works for services, and basic routing. Not a complete Angular course — just enough to answer "what do you know about Angular?" without stalling.
